errors.context: A school wants 20 different pupils from a complete register.
lines: Number every eligible pupil from 1 to 400.
Use a random-number generator set to 1–400.
Keep the first 20 numbers produced, even when a number appears twice.

repairs.text: Keep going until 20 distinct valid numbers have been obtained; ignore repeats.
Replace the generator with a regular interval of 20.
Keep the repeats, but ask those pupils twice.

errors.explanation: Repeated numbers would select the same sampling unit more than once. For a simple random sample without replacement, discard repeats and continue until 20 different pupils have been chosen.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Keeping repeats guarantees 20 distinct pupils because there were 20 draws.
Twenty draws may refer to fewer than 20 different pupils.
A repeated number makes every previously selected pupil ineligible for the study.

impact.explanation: For sampling without replacement, count distinct valid labels, not generator outputs. Repeated labels must be ignored until 20 different pupils are selected.

errors.context: An inspector selects 20 items from a numbered list of 200.
lines: Calculate the interval as 200 ÷ 20 = 10.
Start at item 1 without any random choice.
Take every tenth item until 20 are selected.

repairs.text: Make the interval 20 instead.
Choose a random start from positions 1 to 10, then every tenth item.
Use the first ten items only.

errors.explanation: Systematic sampling needs a random starting position within the first interval (for this exact integer interval). Always starting at 1 makes the choice of start non-random.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Using an interval of ten will always select fewer than 20 items from 200.
Choosing an interval of ten guarantees that each individual item is sampled.
Only one of the ten possible starting positions is used, so many items cannot be selected.

impact.explanation: With k = 10, randomly choose the start from 1 to 10. Fixing it at 1 makes the selection pattern predetermined.

errors.context: A school has separate year-group registers and needs proportional representation.
lines: Divide pupils into non-overlapping year groups.
Calculate the required number from each year group.
Take the first names alphabetically from each group until the target is reached.

repairs.text: Replace the year groups with a single volunteer queue.
Select the specified number randomly within each group, without repeats.
Keep the alphabetical order because the sample sizes are proportional.

errors.explanation: Proportional group numbers alone do not make a sample stratified random: the units within each stratum must be chosen randomly.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Within each year group, surname order determines who is chosen rather than random selection.
The calculation of the number required from each year group becomes impossible.
Alphabetical selection gives all eligible pupils equal probability within each year group.

impact.explanation: Correct proportional group numbers do not fix non-random selection within each stratum.

errors.context: Interviewers have targets of 30 commuters and 20 non-commuters.
lines: Set a numerical target for each group.
Recruit eligible people encountered until each target is filled.
Because the group sizes are fixed, the individuals must have been chosen randomly.

repairs.text: Quota sampling uses non-random selection within groups; targets do not imply random selection.
Interview everyone, so that the investigation becomes a census.
Remove the group targets and only sample every tenth person.

errors.explanation: A quota sets targets but typically fills them by approaching available respondents. Proportional quotas are not the same as random selection within strata.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Meeting a quota is sufficient to make every individual equally likely to be chosen.
The quotas fix group totals but do not make the choice of individuals random.
The two quotas must be equal for this method to count as quota sampling.

impact.explanation: Quota sampling fills preset categories by non-random recruitment; it is not automatically stratified random sampling.

errors.context: A calculator is explicitly programmed to generate integers only from 1 to 150.
lines: Number the 150 eligible people from 1 to 150.
Generate random integers in the inclusive range 1–150.
Reject any number outside 1–150 because this restricted generator regularly produces them.

repairs.text: Use a random starting position and take every tenth person.
Retain all repeats until the sample size is reached.
Discard repeats, but out-of-range rejection is unnecessary with a generator restricted to 1–150.

errors.explanation: A generator constrained to 1–150 cannot produce out-of-range numbers. Ignore repeats; exclude invalid numbers only when the random source can actually produce them.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Restricting the random integers to 1–150 makes repeated values impossible.
The valid range makes it unnecessary to give each eligible person a unique label.
The claimed out-of-range values cannot occur with this restricted generator.

impact.explanation: Range restrictions prevent out-of-range outputs, not repeated outputs. Repeats still need to be ignored when selecting distinct units.

errors.context: A researcher wants a random sample of every club member, including new members.
lines: Obtain last term's register, which excludes the new members.
Assign a unique number to everyone on that old register.
Generate distinct random numbers and contact those people.

repairs.text: Include the new members in a complete up-to-date sampling frame before numbering.
Choose every fifth name in the old register.
Describe the old register as representative because random numbers are used.

errors.explanation: Random selection from an incomplete frame cannot include units that are missing from it. A complete eligible-population frame is essential.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: New club members have zero chance of selection because they are missing from the frame.
Using random numbers makes every new member equally likely to be chosen anyway.
An older list makes the random numbers themselves non-uniform.

impact.explanation: Uniform selection within a frame cannot repair omissions from the frame; coverage of the target population is incomplete.

errors.context: A school has 300 Year 12 and 200 Year 13 pupils. A proportional sample of 50 is wanted.
lines: Separate the two year groups.
Allocate 25 places to Year 12 and 25 to Year 13 because there are two strata.
Randomly select the allocated number from each year-group register.

repairs.text: Take 50 from each year group.
Allocate 30 to Year 12 and 20 to Year 13, then sample randomly within each.
Use 25 each but label it proportional because there are two groups.

errors.explanation: Proportional allocation is 50×300/500=30 and 50×200/500=20. Equal allocation is not proportional when the group sizes differ.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Year 12 is overrepresented: its share in the sample is larger than 60%.
Year 13 is overrepresented: its sample share is 50%, but its population share is 40%.
Equal numbers from each year group are proportional because there are two groups.

impact.explanation: The sample should contain 30 Year 12 and 20 Year 13 pupils, reflecting the 60%/40% population split.

errors.context: A survey team plans a sample from a complete population list.
lines: Number the population and select distinct numbers randomly.
Apply the resulting sample to the survey.
A simple random sample is guaranteed to be representative because it is random.

repairs.text: Random sampling removes every possible bias, so the claim is correct.
A census never has response errors, unlike sampling.
Random selection gives a probability design but does not guarantee a representative realised sample.

errors.explanation: Random selection can produce an unbalanced sample by chance, and nonresponse can introduce bias. Representativeness is not guaranteed.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Random selection forces every subgroup to be included in its exact population proportion.
An unbalanced result proves that the original random-number generator was unfair.
A valid random sample may still underrepresent some subgroups by chance.

impact.explanation: Random sampling gives an appropriate probability mechanism, not a guarantee about the composition of the realised sample.

errors.context: A factory's packing list follows a repeating colour sequence every 10 items.
lines: Order the full list and choose an interval of 10.
Use a random start within the first ten positions.
The random start ensures the repeating list order cannot cause a distorted sample.

repairs.text: A random start does not eliminate a periodicity risk; investigate or change the ordering/design.
Always start at item 1 to prevent periodicity.
Choose a quota sample but call it systematic.

errors.explanation: When the sampling interval matches a periodic pattern, one start may select only one phase of the pattern. Check for periodic ordering.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: All selected items may belong to the same phase of the repeating ten-item sequence.
A random start always includes a balanced selection of every phase of the sequence.
Selecting every tenth item prevents any of the listed colours from being sampled.

impact.explanation: A random start alone cannot remove the periodicity risk when a sampling interval matches a repeated list pattern.

errors.context: A travel survey sets 40 morning and 60 afternoon respondent targets.
lines: Decide and communicate the two quotas.
Recruit the first eligible volunteers available in each period.
Classify the method as stratified random because it has two groups.

repairs.text: The use of a survey makes the method a census.
It is quota sampling: there is no random selection of individuals within each group.
It is simple random because group targets were set.

errors.explanation: Having groups is insufficient to make a design stratified random. Without random selection within the groups, this is quota sampling.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Any use of two groups makes the selection random within each group.
The chosen individuals are recruited non-randomly, even though the quotas are filled.
Using volunteers means group totals cannot be specified in advance.

impact.explanation: Group targets are not the distinguishing feature of stratified random sampling; random selection within groups is.

errors.context: A researcher needs 40 from an ordered register of 197.
lines: The planned ratio N/n is 197/40 = 4.925.
Choose a random start of 1 from the first five positions, then take every fifth entry; this particular start gives 40 entries.
Claim that rounding N/n to the nearest integer is the universal systematic rule and always returns the requested n.

repairs.text: Start at 1 and keep the rounded rule, which always works.
A non-integer ratio needs a deliberately specified suitable systematic pattern and count check; no universal rounding rule exists.
Ignore all people after the first 40 entries.

errors.explanation: Starting at 1 gives 40 entries, but other possible starts can give only 39. Rounding the interval is not a universal rule for a non-integer N/n; check how the proposed scheme achieves the required number.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Every start from 1 to 5 gives exactly 40 selected positions from 197.
A non-integer population-to-sample ratio prevents any systematic sample being taken.
With every fifth entry, some starting positions select only 39, not the requested 40.

impact.explanation: For 197 entries and every fifth selection, starts 1 or 2 give 40; starts 3, 4 or 5 give 39. The method must specify and check how to obtain 40.

errors.context: A school wants views from all students but asks only students in the canteen at 12:30.
lines: Define the target population as all students.
Ask those who are available at the canteen at 12:30.
Conclude that this gives an unbiased picture of all students because it is easy to carry out.

repairs.text: Treat the canteen group as an opportunity sample with possible time/location selection bias; broaden recruitment.
Describe all pupils at school as having been observed.
Choose every fifth canteen visitor and claim all students are equally likely.

errors.explanation: Being available at a particular place and time may correlate with the behaviour being studied and exclude groups. Ease is not representativeness.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Students absent from the canteen at that time have no opportunity to be selected.
Everyone in the school has an equal chance because the canteen is on campus.
An opportunity sample is a census as long as the interviewer asks everyone nearby.

impact.explanation: Selection is restricted to one place and time. Students elsewhere may differ from canteen users, creating possible coverage bias.

errors.context: A survey aims for 55 out of 550, with strata sizes 205, 190 and 155.
lines: Allocate approximately 20.5, 19 and 15.5 places to the three strata.
Allocate 21, 19 and 15 whole-number places, totalling 55.
Randomly take 21, 19 and 16 people from the strata and report a sample size of 55.

repairs.text: Take the first 55 names regardless of strata.
Round all three down and sample only 54 people.
Draw the allocated 21, 19 and 15 people randomly within the respective strata, totalling 55.

errors.explanation: Although the intended allocation 21 + 19 + 15 = 55 is defensible, the proposed draw 21 + 19 + 16 = 56. The final draw must match whole-number allocations summing to 55.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: The specified selection totals only 54, so the sample is too small.
The specified selection totals 56, exceeding the intended sample size of 55.
Proportional stratified samples must have equal numbers drawn from every stratum.

impact.explanation: 21 + 19 + 16 = 56. A defensible whole-number allocation such as 21, 19, 15 totals 55; the actual draw must use those totals.

errors.context: A researcher uses an unrestricted random-digit table for numbers 001–180.
lines: Create a full numbered frame 001 to 180.
Read three-digit groups from the random-digit table.
Retain values such as 000 and 924 as valid selections, as long as they have not appeared before.

repairs.text: Keep all values if no duplicate appears.
Reject values outside 001–180 and any repeats; continue until enough distinct units are chosen.
Replace the sampling frame with only the first 100 units.

errors.explanation: Unlike a constrained 1–180 generator, a random-digit table can produce invalid values. Reject out-of-range values and repeats.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Three-digit random tables are incapable of producing 000.
A random table makes repeated labels acceptable in a sample without replacement.
000 and 924 do not identify anybody in the numbered population 001–180.

impact.explanation: Reject groups outside 001–180 as well as repeats when reading unrestricted random digits, and keep sampling until enough distinct valid labels appear.

errors.context: An investigation compares the breakfast habits of all town residents.
lines: Interview the first 30 willing shoppers at one supermarket on Monday morning.
Record their responses accurately.
Describe the survey as covering the target population equally because the sample is convenient.

repairs.text: Convenience alone makes it representative if n=30.
Treat the result as an opportunity sample with likely coverage and nonresponse limitations; sample at other times/places or use a suitable frame.
Claim all town residents are equally likely to visit that supermarket at that time.

errors.explanation: The recruited people are only those available and willing at one place and time, not a random cross-section of all town residents.

impact.question: What is the mathematical consequence of this mistake?

options.text: Residents who do not shop there at that time may be excluded, making representation uncertain.
Recording accurate responses guarantees that the selection of shoppers was random.
A sample of 30 guarantees that the town's demographic groups are represented.

impact.explanation: Recording responses accurately does not correct a convenience-based sampling frame. Other times, sites or probability methods could broaden coverage.
